justification: Fresh judgement first. Against what ranks for 'sql joins explained' (Coding Horror: a 3-minute Venn-diagram post on two 4-row name tables, no multiplicity, no ON-vs-WHERE, no NOT IN; jOOQ 'Say NO to Venn Diagrams': the same thesis on author/book tables, but it stops at cross/inner/outer and has no NULL-key treatment, no fan-out bug, no anti/semi joins, no algorithms, no exercises; Microsoft Learn Joins: authoritative 4,000-word reference, AdventureWorks snippets, no row-level picture, not a teaching page; Atlassian's page would not render for me and is not counted), this article is clearly the most useful page for a learner. Its original value is concrete: an own member/loan/payment dataset built so that two rows cause every bug; a COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) hook that is shown failing twice before it is explained; five purpose-built SVGs (match lines, the 20-cell ON grid with NULL cells, the bracket figure, the self-join figure, the 2x2 fan-out); the ON-vs-WHERE bug and its mirror image both executed; the double-SUM fan-out bug with a test that passes on Chen; an INTERSECT-versus-JOIN row-count test I found in no competitor; the NOT IN/NULL trap expanded line by line; a LINQ null-key aside tied to dotnet/runtime source; and a costed algorithm section that ties k back to row multiplication. No filler: the first sentence poses the task, there is no intro/outro boilerplate, no summary, and the page ends on content. No keyword stuffing; title and description read as human. Templating: I compared headings, openings and exercise formats with complexity/amortized-analysis and version-control/how-git-works. Openings are three different moves (scenario, documentation paradox, three numbers); no heading is shared; exercises here are find-the-bug mid-article, a paper count with the query and output inside the solution, and a write-the-query task, each placed after the section it tests, with no terminal 'Exercises' section. Shared elements (pitfall and dotnet callouts, collapsed solutions) are site furniture, not article template. Machine-text check: paragraph lengths vary widely, contrast constructions ('not false but NULL', 'the definition, not the way it is computed') carry content, the one explicit triplet ('for three reasons') lists three distinct, checkable reasons, and there is no empty signposting. Plagiarism: five distinctive sentences searched in quotes ('One line is one result row', 'An overlap can never be larger than the smaller circle', 'padding belongs to the join step' / 'which lines are drawn rather than which finished rows survive', 'a small cross product hidden inside an ordinary-looking join', 'One NULL anywhere in the subquery empties the entire result') returned no verbatim or near-verbatim match; nearest hits (boringSQL, a DEV post) explain the well-known NOT IN fact in other words on other data. Against cited sources: I re-opened Microsoft Learn Joins, PostgreSQL xoper-optimization and SQLite optoverview; every quoted fragment is verbatim and short ('can't be directly expressed with Transact-SQL syntax', nulls 'don't match each other', 'must represent equality', 'behave like equality', 'almost the same thing as a hash join', outer joins 'will not be reordered', CROSS JOIN never reordered, build input is the smaller, index nested loops fastest for small outer/large indexed inner, adaptive join defers the choice), attributed and hyperlinked at the claim; none of the sources' example tables or running examples are reused. No invented experience or statistics; the round-1 frequency assertions are gone. Rendered page (verify-page --drafts --no-lighthouse): 0 broken links, 0 console errors, 0 px mobile overflow, only failure the known NEEDS_MARKUS placeholder; after Sources there is a 'Keep reading' block (pillar, all topics, start here, glossary), so it is not a dead end, and docs/crosslinks/databases/sql-joins.md exists with eight sensible, precisely located targets plus inbound suggestions. Round-1 check (all three critics, blockers/majors): (1) 'Exercises' ending with 'Predict the...' first item: really fixed, section removed and exercises redistributed; (2) exercise gave away n = 6: fixed, query and output now inside the solution; (3) unscoped 'SQL has no ANTI JOIN keyword': fixed, scoped to the four named engines with Spark SQL cited as the counter-example, same for semi-join; (4) five uncited sources: all fifteen front-matter sources are now cited inline where they support a claim (MySQL FULL JOIN and <=>, T-SQL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM from 2022, PostgreSQL planner and HASHES/MERGES), and the portability caveats the technical critic asked for are in the body; (5) dead end / no crosslinks file: fixed; (6) algorithm costs and conditions: fixed, each of the three has cost, applicability and the k term; (7) design majors (Figure 5 header collision, missing Figure 4, clipped operative code): figure numbering is now 1-5 with a new self-join figure, headers are pay_id/amount, and statements are re-broken to about 40 columns (design critic to confirm visually). Minors also addressed: citations are links, RIGHT JOIN is executed, provenance sentence reduced to reproduction instructions, mirror-image ON bug shown, preference for NOT EXISTS justified, INTERSECT argument reordered, empty NOT IN result shown as COUNT 0, NOT IN expansion moved into a block inside a pitfall. None of these was papered over. Why 9.0 and not higher: what remains is nit-level (an overloaded final paragraph, 'a few analytics engines' resting on one citation, a Theta/'big-O terms' wording mismatch, a beginner label on a page whose last section assumes B-trees and hashing). I hold short of 10 because the core thesis is shared with a well-known existing post (jOOQ), so the page is clearly deeper and better illustrated than the ranking results rather than novel in argument.

issues.location: Last paragraph of 'What the engine does instead of building every pair' (begins 'SQL Server's page adds an adaptive variant')
issues.problem: One eight-sentence paragraph carries five separate points (adaptive joins, optimizer picks method and order, inner-join spellings interchangeable in SQLite, outer joins and CROSS JOIN are exceptions, advice on spelling, index candidate). It is the page's last impression and reads as a catch-all of round-1 fixes rather than a designed ending.
issues.fixLooksLike: Split into two short paragraphs: one on who chooses the algorithm and order (adaptive join, optimizer), one on what that means for the spelling you pick and its two exceptions; keep the closing index sentence as its own line so the page ends on the link to the planned indexes article.

issues.location: 'Anti-joins: finding the rows with no match', first paragraph: 'a few analytics engines do, and Spark SQL, for one, accepts LEFT ANTI JOIN'
issues.problem: 'A few' is a plural claim supported by a single citation. It is true (DuckDB, ClickHouse, Impala), but under the brief's cite-where-claimed rule the plural is unsourced.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either say only what is cited ('some engines do: Spark SQL accepts LEFT ANTI JOIN') or add one more primary link (for example the DuckDB or ClickHouse JOIN reference) after opening it.

issues.location: 'What the engine does...', paragraph after the C# program: 'Theta(n * m) in big-O terms'
issues.problem: A Theta bound is labelled 'big-O terms' to hang the glossary link on; a careful reader sees two different notations equated. Small, but it is the sort of seam a reviewer reads as unedited text.
issues.fixLooksLike: Reword so the link text fits, e.g. 'exactly n * m times, which is Theta(n * m) (see big-O notation in the glossary for the family of notations)', or state it as O(n * m) and note it is also a lower bound for this loop.

issues.location: Front matter 'level: beginner' versus the final section (B-tree lookups, hash build/probe, merge, grace partitioning, Theta/O with k)
issues.problem: The first three quarters are genuinely beginner material; the last section assumes data-structure background. The glossary links soften this, but the label slightly oversells accessibility of the whole page.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one sentence at the top of the last section telling a beginner it is optional on first reading and what it presupposes (hash tables, sorted merge, logarithms), or set level to the site's beginner-to-intermediate equivalent if one exists.
